rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous verse highlights these servants' public conduct; this one turns to their private life.
rows.anchor: The previous verse points to a certain trait of the servants of the Most Merciful related to their public life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prostrating and standing expresses more than obligatory prayer: they eagerly keep night vigil and seek forgiveness instead of sleeping in luxury.
rows.anchor: It also refers to their great fondness and intense keenness for the night vigil in the tahajjud prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's punishment is adhesive and impossible to escape once it seizes someone, so seeking protection from it at night is far-sighted; escape can only be sought in this world with God's help.
rows.anchor: such is the adhesive nature of this punishment that it is impossible to escape from it once it seizes a person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He distinguishes the two terms for abode: one means a permanent resting place and the other a temporary stay, either of which in Hell is intolerable.
rows.anchor: the former is used for a permanent resting place and the latter for a temporary one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They avoid both extravagance and miserliness because others have rights in their wealth, and they limit their needs to meet those rights.
rows.anchor: They are not extravagant in their spending because they know that others have a right in their wealth too.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A moderate standard of living varies with circumstances, but a person can judge one suited to their society that leaves room to serve the underprivileged and religion.
rows.anchor: he can ascertain his own standard of living that affords him the opportunity to serve the underprivileged as well as his religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forefathers' example is to spend as much as possible for God's cause instead of raising one's lifestyle; this spending is not extravagance.
rows.anchor: instead of raising their own standard of living, they should spend for the cause of God as much as possible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those insatiably seeking a higher standard become Satan's brothers and neglect their brethren's rights; when widespread, this social ailment ends in socialism.
rows.anchor: they become the brothers of Satan and they never have the urge to fulfil the rights of their brethren.

rows.speaker: Al-Jawharī
rows.claim: Al-Jawharī defines athām as the consequence of a sin.
rows.anchor: Al-Jawharī says that the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression describes a noun or verb arising from its consequence, as in the Quranic phrase about meeting ghayy.
rows.anchor: This usage refers to the meaning of a noun or a verb that arises from its consequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God regards every life as sacred, barring legal immunity for someone guilty of a crime; murder, polytheism, and fornication are the greatest offenses against God and humanity, agreed upon by scriptures, and the servants avoid them.
rows.anchor: God has regarded every life to be sacred and it is prohibited to commit excesses against it except if that person is guilty of a crime.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laghw means engagements that are not befitting to serious and mature people.
rows.anchor: engagements that are not befitting to serious and mature people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links the servants' dignified passing by frivolous things to 28:55, which describes ignoring nonsensical talk and avoiding entanglement with the ignorant.
rows.anchor: In verse 55 of Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ, this trait is stated thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disgrace intensifies the horror of punishment, and the Quraysh hear this warning because eternal humiliation is the true punishment of arrogance.
rows.anchor: the real punishment of arrogance is eternal humiliation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance, faith, and righteous deeds replace a person's past evil deeds with good; the conditions and etiquette of repentance are treated at 4:17-18.
rows.anchor: The good deeds of people who repent and profess faith and do righteous deeds replace their evil ones done in the past.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repentant return to God triumphantly, in contrast to the sinner who bears the consequences described in 25:68; the indefinite noun magnifies the return as grand and majestic.
rows.anchor: In other words, this return would be very grand and majestic.

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: In the lost-sheep parable, Jesus teaches God's joy at a penitent person and the great reward God gives them; Islahi sees the same meaning here.
rows.anchor: In the parable of the lost sheep, Jesus (sws) has very eloquently taught how happy God becomes on a penitent person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse encourages those anxious about leaving a sinful life and company: they gain God's company and blessings and need nothing else.
rows.anchor: those who leave sin and their sinful company acquire the company and blessings of God and those who acquire this need nothing else.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He defines falsehood and frivolous engagements as things unfit for serious, mature people, and says the servants pass them like a hygiene-loving person passes filth.
rows.anchor: The verse says that servants of the Most Merciful God pass by frivolous things the way a hygiene-loving person passes by a filthy place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse praises the servants of the Most Merciful while sarcastically rebuking Qur'an opponents who listen only to make objections; the same topic appears at 72:19 and 70:36-37.
rows.anchor: This verse simultaneously praises the servants of the Most Merciful God and passes a sarcastic remark on the blind and deaf opponents of the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet says each person is a shepherd accountable for their flock; Islahi cites al-Bukhārī, hadith 2554.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servants care about their family's afterlife and Satan's path rather than worldly pleasures alone, continually praying for conduct pleasing to God; this echoes the family's fear in 52:26.
rows.anchor: Before this, we remained fearful about our families.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer for being made leaders of the righteous is not a request to obtain leadership; it concerns properly carrying out the leadership responsibilities every family head has.
rows.anchor: this prayer does not relate to procuring leadership; it, in fact, relates to befittingly carrying out the responsibilities of the position of leadership every head of the family actually possesses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their humble, down-to-earth lives earn them lofty ranks in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: they spent their lives in a very humble and down to earth way. For this reason, they will be bestowed with such high ranks in the hereafter

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Jesus is reported to promise that the meek will inherit the earth, a parallel to the reward of the humble described here.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) is reported to have said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'because of their perseverance' signals that cultivating and maintaining these traits requires steadfastness and is difficult.
rows.anchor: engendering these traits and sustaining them is not an easy task; it needs a lot of steadfastness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised salutations and greetings mean that angels welcome those who pass the test.
rows.anchor: those who pass this test will indeed be worthy of being greeted and welcomed by angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pleasant description of Paradise as a place to live and stay contrasts with the earlier description of Hell.
rows.anchor: nice will it be a place to live and stay” occur in contrast with the words mentioned for Hell earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing threat tells Qur'an opponents that God does not need them; the Prophet calls them to truth solely for their own benefit.
rows.anchor: it is not because without them some of God’s tasks will be left unfulfilled. God does not need them in any way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they deny the message, its consequence will soon arrive under God's established practice toward those who deny messengers.
rows.anchor: if they deny this message, they should be prepared to face its consequences that are bound to happen very soon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Shu‘arā’ is the counterpart of al-Furqān and shares its essential theme: affirming Muḥammad's messengership and the Qur'an's divinity, though its arguments and discourse style differ.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is the counterpart of Sūrah Furqān that precedes it. For this reason, there is no basic difference between the theme of both.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic narratives mentioned concisely in al-Furqān are retold in greater detail here.
rows.anchor: The anecdotes of the prophets of God that were rather concisely mentioned in the previous sūrah are mentioned in more detail in this one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah especially rebuts Quraysh accusations that the Prophet is a soothsayer and sorcerer.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh used to accuse the Prophet (sws) of being a soothsayer and a sorcerer. This accusation is specially dispelled.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain after each narrative targets those demanding a punishment sign and directs them to learn from the fate of earlier peoples who denied messengers.
rows.anchor: This repetition shows that those who were demanding a sign of punishment from the Prophet (sws) as proof of his veracity are specially addressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening reassures the Prophet about deniers and demands for a sign: the Qur'an is self-evident, the universe already contains signs, and God is powerful yet merciful in granting respite.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān does not need any external proof for its veracity: it is a proof of itself. If these people deny it, they will face each and every threat it is warning them of.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The main body briefly recounts Moses' story from his arrival before Pharaoh until the drowning, ending with the recurring refrain.
rows.anchor: Events that took place from the time he came to the Pharaoh until the time he was drowned are briefly narrated.
